title: US FDA Botanical Drug Development Guidance for Industry
official_citation: FDA-2015-D-0648; Botanical Drug Development Guidance for Industry (21 CFR Part 312)
summary: Specific regulatory pathway for botanical products intended to be marketed as prescription drugs in the United States, accommodating batch-to-batch variation in complex plant mixtures.
key_clauses: Botanical Drug Definition: Products that consist of vegetable materials (plant parts, algae, microscopic fungi, or combinations thereof) intended for use in disease diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention.

Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC): Rigorous raw material sourcing controls (GACP - Good Agricultural and Collection Practices), spectroscopic fingerprinting (HPLC, LC-MS), and biological assays are required.

Clinical Trial Pathway: Phase 1 human safety trials may rely on documented prior human experience (such as centuries of Ayurvedic usage in India) to support initial safety without full conventional animal toxicology, but Phase 2 & Phase 3 pivotal trials must satisfy FDA efficacy endpoints.
Dietary Supplement Pathway (DSHEA 1994): If marketed without therapeutic drug claims, can be sold as dietary supplement under 21 CFR Part 111 cGMP with structure/function claims only.
practical_guidance: For US expansion, decide early: Dietary Supplement (DSHEA - fast entry, no cure claims) vs Botanical Prescription Drug (NDA pathway - requires $20M+ multi-center clinical trials, but unlocks prescription exclusivity and insurance reimbursement).

title: EU Directive 2004/24/EC - Traditional Herbal Medicinal Products (THMPD)
authority: European Medicines Agency (EMA) - Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC)
official_citation: Directive 2004/24/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council
summary: Simplified registration procedure for traditional herbal medicinal products fulfilling specific criteria regarding duration of safe traditional medical use.
key_clauses: 30-Year Usage Criterion: Requires evidence that the medicinal product or corresponding product has been in medicinal use throughout a period of at least 30 years preceding the application, including at least 15 years within the European Union.
Non-EU Herbal Traditions: Ayurvedic medicines face hurdles for 15-year EU usage requirement unless documented EU distributor records exist, or European Community herbal monographs exist.
Indications: Exclusively suitable for self-medication without medical supervision (no injectable, prescription-only, or severe disease treatment permitted).

Full Well-Established Use (WEU): If 10 years of well-established medical use in EU with recognized efficacy (bibliographic data as per Directive 2001/83/EC Article 10a) can be demonstrated, full marketing authorization is available.
practical_guidance: Exporters should collaborate with EU entities possessing documented 15-year import records or file under Food Supplement legislation (EFSA) where harmonized permitted botanicals exist.

title: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge
summary: Historic global treaty establishing mandatory disclosure requirements for patent applicants worldwide whose inventions are based on genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge.
key_clauses: Mandatory Patent Disclosure: Patent applicants worldwide must disclose the country of origin of genetic resources or the indigenous/local community that provided traditional knowledge.
Information Systems & TK Databases: Establishes interoperable databases (modeled on India's TKDL) accessible to patent examiners worldwide (USPTO, EPO, JPO, CNIPA) to prevent misappropriation.
Sanctions & Remedies: Failure to disclose provides grounds for administrative queries, post-grant review, and in fraudulent cases, revocation of patent rights.
practical_guidance: Global startups utilizing Ayurvedic bio-resources must maintain transparent supply chain chain-of-custody documentation to satisfy mandatory WIPO disclosure when filing PCT applications.
